newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi to license big foreign projects by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi to license big foreign projects by year-end.

text.p: Vietnam will license a number of big foreign investment projects by the end of the year, including the country's first oil refinery, the Vice-Minister for Planning and Investment said in an interview published on Friday.

"Between now and the end of the year it is certain that the government will license a number of large projects such as Dung Quat oil refinery No. 1, the Quang Ninh 300 MW thermo-power plant and a Vietnam-Hyundai shipbuilding yard," Nguyen Nhac told the Saigon Times weekly magazine.
Vietnam's state oil and gas firm Petrovietnam and a clutch of foreign partners agreed in March on a feasibility study to build Dung Quat refinery in the central Quang Ngai province.

The 130,00 barrels per day project has long been considered controversial because the site chosen is an undeveloped area 1,000 km (600 miles) north of the country's oilfields and chief consumption base.
French oil firm Total SA pulled out of the project last year, branding it economically unviable.
Petrovietnam and a consortium led by South Korea's LG Group each took a 30-percent share in the feasibility study. The U.S. firm Stone & Webster took three percent out of LG's 30 percent.

Two Taiwanese firms, Chinese Petroleum Corp and Chinese Investment Development Corp, shared 10 percent while Malaysia's state oil firm Petronas split 30 percent equally with the U.S. refiner Conoco Inc, a unit of DuPont Co
The government hopes Dung Quat will be operating by 2000 and is now planning to build a second refinery, of about the same capacity, probably in the north of the country.

Power industry sources said earlier this month that U.S. firm Oxbow International Power Corp had been singled out for talks on a roughly $300 million coal-fired electricity generating plant in Vietnam's northern province of Quang Ninh.
The 300 MW plant, to which Nhac was referring in the magazine interview, would be Vietnam's first build- operate-transfer (BOT) power project.
He also referred to a $95.39 million shipyard project in which four companies belonging to Hyundai Mipo Dockyard Co would have a 70 percent stake.
Nhac said that in the period from January 1 to August 20, his ministry had licensed 186 projects worth $4.35 billion, a slight decline from $4.57 billion in the same period of 1995.
However, he said the value of applications for projects in the first seven months and 20 days of the year stood at $7.25 billion compared with $4.94 billion in the same period last year.
Vietnam approved a record $7.4 billion worth of projects backed with investment from abroad in 1995.
